- Overestimate prices after recent spikes, especially when sentiment is high (positive sentiment > 0.5) — model tends to overshoot and fail to correct quickly.
- Underestimate prices when sentiment is negative or low (sentiment < 0.3) — model is overly optimistic or fails to recognize downward pressure.
- Model exhibits mean reversion bias: forecasts often overshoot recent highs and undershoot recent lows, especially in the first 5–10 days of the forecast horizon.
- When sentiment is trending upward, model tends to overreact to short-term volatility and overweights momentum — suppress early forecast spikes if sentiment is weak or neutral.
- For 30-day forecasts, model consistently overestimates the first 5–7 days, then gradually converges — adjust early forecast values downward if sentiment is weak or shows signs of cooling.
- If sentiment is high and price is rising, model often fails to account for policy or market correction — reduce forecast peak by 5–10% if sentiment > 0.7 and price > 70.
- Sentiment decay (e.g., sentiment dropping from 0.8 to 0.3) should trigger a downward correction in forecast, especially if price is above 70 — model often ignores sentiment decay until it’s too late.
